record.paper_title: Aspects of Nonabelian Group Based Cryptography: A Survey and Open Problems
record.original_question: Can the security of the non-commutative cryptographic protocols surveyed in the paper be analyzed rigorously?

evidence.quote: 5. Can we analyze the security of this protocols?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider the family of public-key cryptographic protocols whose security is based on algorithmic problems in finitely generated non-abelian groups. Representative examples include:

(a) The Anshel–Anshel–Goldfeld key-exchange protocol, whose security rests on variants of the simultaneous conjugacy search problem in a non-abelian group G: given tuples (a_1,...,a_n) and (b a_1 b^{-1},...,b a_n b^{-1}) of elements of G, recover an element b' such that b' a_i b'^{-1} = b a_i b^{-1} for all i.

(b) The Ko–Lee–Cheon–Han–Kang–Park protocol and related Diffie–Hellman-type schemes in braid groups B_n and other non-abelian platform groups, whose security rests on the conjugacy search problem (given x and y = g x g^{-1} in G, find g) and the decomposition / generalized conjugacy search problems in distinguished subgroups.

(c) Protocols based on the word problem, the membership problem, or the twisted conjugacy problem in platform groups such as braid groups, Thompson's group F, polycyclic groups, Grigorchuk groups, and finitely generated linear (matrix) groups.

Provide a rigorous security analysis of these non-abelian group-based cryptographic protocols. Specifically:

1. For each protocol, identify the precise computational problem P (in a specified platform group G with a specified distribution on instances) whose hardness is necessary and sufficient for the protocol's security under a stated adversarial model (passive eavesdropper, chosen-plaintext, chosen-ciphertext).

2. Establish, with proof, either (i) a polynomial-time reduction from a well-studied hard problem to P, thereby giving a provable security guarantee, or (ii) a polynomial-time algorithm (deterministic, randomized, or generic-case / heuristic with rigorous success-probability bounds) that breaks P on the instance distribution used by the protocol.

3. In particular, determine the worst-case and generic-case computational complexity of the conjugacy search problem, the simultaneous conjugacy search problem, and the decomposition problem in the platform groups listed in (a)–(c), and decide whether each protocol admits a rigorous proof of security or a rigorous polynomial-time attack.
artifact.status_search_result: Surveys and monographs from 2011 onward (e.g., Myasnikov–Shpilrain–Ushakov's AMS volume on non-commutative cryptography, the 2016 polycyclic-group survey on arXiv, and later surveys of public-key cryptography over non-abelian groups) consistently note that rigorous security proofs for the main non-abelian group-based protocols are lacking, and that the precise complexity (in particular generic-case complexity) of the underlying conjugacy-type search problems in platform groups such as braid groups and polycyclic groups remains unresolved. Specific schemes (e.g., the original Ko–Lee braid-group protocol) have been broken by length-based and linear-representation attacks, but a unified rigorous security analysis of the surveyed family of protocols is still considered an open problem.

status_evidence.title: The Status of Polycyclic Group-Based Cryptography: A Survey and Open Problems
status_evidence.snippet: The complexity of the search conjugacy problem in polycyclic groups is unknown, but widely conjectured to be hard.
status_evidence.claim: The complexity of the central hard problem underlying polycyclic-group cryptography is still open.

status_evidence.title: Non-commutative cryptography - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: Security of various protocols is based on the difficulty of the conjugacy decision problem and the conjugacy search problem; many proposals have been cryptanalyzed but no general rigorous security proofs are available.
status_evidence.claim: No general rigorous security analysis of non-abelian group-based protocols is currently established.

status_evidence.title: Non-Commutative Cryptography and Complexity of Group-Theoretic Problems (Myasnikov–Shpilrain–Ushakov)
status_evidence.snippet: Monograph surveying complexity of group-theoretic problems used in cryptography and listing open complexity questions.
status_evidence.claim: Standard reference indicating the complexity foundations of these protocols remain partially open.
